content: Materials science examines the relationships between material composition, structure, processing, and resulting properties, enabling engineers to select and design materials for specific applications. Mechanical properties characterize how materials respond to applied forces: strength measures resistance to deformation or failure under load, with distinct metrics including tensile strength (resistance to pulling forces), compressive strength (resistance to pushing forces), and yield strength (limit before permanent deformation occurs); elasticity reflects a material's ability to return to original shape after deformation, quantified by Young's modulus (ratio of stress to strain); and toughness indicates energy absorption before fracture, distinguishing brittle materials like ceramics from ductile ones like metals. Atomic and microstructure fundamentally determine these propertiesâmetals derive strength from crystalline structures where atoms arrange in regular patterns, with dislocations and grain boundaries influencing performance; ceramics feature strong ionic or covalent bonds creating hardness and heat resistance but susceptibility to brittle fracture; polymers consist of long molecular chains with properties determined by chain length, branching, and cross-linking; and composites combine different materials to achieve properties unavailable from single materials, like fiber-reinforced polymers using strong fibers embedded in flexible matrices. Environmental factors significantly affect material performance: corrosion degrades metals through electrochemical reactions with environments; UV radiation breaks polymer bonds, causing embrittlement and color fading; temperature extremes alter mechanical properties with most materials weakening at high temperatures and becoming brittle at low temperatures; and moisture absorption affects dimensional stability and strength particularly in hygroscopic materials like wood and concrete. Material selection balances performance requirements against constraints including cost, weight, manufacturability, and sustainability, often requiring compromise across competing priorities.

scenario.title: Bridge Design Laboratory
scenario.content: Students design and test bridges using various materials with realistic physical properties, analyzing how material choices affect structural performance. The simulation allows students to select materials ranging from traditional options (wood, steel, concrete) to advanced composites, adjusting composition and processing parameters to modify properties. The system visualizes internal forces, stress distributions, and failure modes under different loading conditions, showing concepts like tension, compression, shear, and bending in real-time. Students can subject their designs to environmental challenges including temperature fluctuations, corrosive conditions, and repeated loading cycles to assess long-term durability. Interactive tools demonstrate material behavior at multiple scales, from atomic structures to macroscopic properties, helping students connect microscopic arrangements with engineering performance. Challenge scenarios require students to design bridges for specific constraints like budget limitations, weight restrictions, extreme environments, or unusual loading conditions, teaching materials selection principles through practical engineering applications.

hypothesis.description: Students will analyze material behavior by examining the relationship between structure and properties. They will predict how different materials respond to mechanical forces and environmental conditions, and select appropriate materials for specific engineering applications based on performance requirements and constraints.
